sources.section: Treatment › Particular cases › Infants (babies under 1 year-old) › Unconscious infants
sources.text:
Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in children less than one year old because they can cause liver damage.[59]

An unconscious infant has to be placed face-up on a firm and horizontal surface (as the floor). The baby's head must be in a straight position, facing frontally, because tilting it too much backwards can close the windpipe (trachea) in infants.

Emergency medical services should be summoned, and an automated external defibrillator (AED) should be retrieved.

Until emergency services arrive, the American Heart Association[59] recommends starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) adapted to infants (<1 year old). It is a cycle of resuscitation[60] that alternates compressions and rescue breaths, like in a normal CPR, but with some differences:
The rescuer begins by making 30 compressions, pressing, with two thumbs or the heel of one's hand, on the lower half of the bone in the middle of the chest (the sternum, on its part that is the nearest to the belly), at an approximate rate of nearly 2 per second (100-120 compressions per minute).

At the end of the round of compressions, the rescuer looks into the mouth for the obstructing object. And, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it (usually using a finger sweep). The rescuer must not confuse a foreign object with epiglottis: a cartilaginous flap of the throat, nor with uvula: a piece of flesh in the back of the mouth. Current protocols do not recommend attempting to extract the object if it is not visible (a blind extraction) because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident. In total, no more than ten seconds should be spent without doing compressions. If the object cannot be immediately extracted, this CPR procedure must continue to the next action and continue until the babies can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

In the next step of the CPR, the rescuer makes a rescue breath, covering the baby's mouth and nose simultaneously with their own mouth, and gently exhaling one time. The goal of a rescue breath is to observe the rise and fall of the chest, indicating that air has reached the lungs. However, one should be careful so as to not overinflate the baby's lungs; a rescuer should not attempt to blow against resistance. After two rescue breaths, the rescuer must return to the 30 initial compressions, repeating the same resuscitation cycle again, continually, until the choking baby regains consciousness and begins to breathe normally, or until emergency help arrives.

Defibrillation may be needed, as a choking infant that is already unconscious can suffer a cardiac arrest at any moment due to hypoxia.[52] AEDs, which are available in many public places, are designed to be safe and easy to use; they announce instructions with voice messages, and the device will not shock a patient who does not require defibrillation. One of the pads of the AED is attached to the baby's chest, and the other pad to the baby's back.

sources.original_text:
A choking victim who becomes unconscious[3][48][49] must be gently caught before falling and placed lying face-up on a surface.[50] That surface should be firm enough (it is recommended placing a layer of something on the floor and laying the victim above).

Emergency medical services should be summoned, if this has not already been done.

It can be also convenient that any rescuer asks for a defibrillator around (an AED, as those devices are commonplace), just in case it can be necessary to treat the victim's heart.

Chest compressions of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), proper rhythm.

The anti-choking cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for unconscious adults and children is quite similar to any other CPR, but with some modifications:

In a first step, a series of 30 chest compressions are applied on the lower half of the sternum (the bone that is along the middle of the chest from the neck to the belly) at an approximate rhythm of nearly 2 per second.

After that series, the rescuer looks for the obstructing object and, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it, usually by using a finger sweeping (hopefully from the mouth). Normally, the object would be a food bolus (and not the epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap of the throat). It is also possible to try to extract it when it is deeper and not visible, always carefully: using the fingers to take it, or lifting the victim's chin to form a straight way to the throat while the victim is face up (face down in case of the victim's tongue obstructs too much, or on a side with a base under the head) and then grasping or sweeping the stuck object with tools: thin kitchen tweezers, scissors (these used with care), forks and spoons (in a reverse position: introducing their handle) or even a toothpick (if other instruments were too big for the case); however, the protocols do not recommend extracting the obstructing object if it is not visible (a blind extraction), because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident, and because the compressions could move the object outside by themselves (in some cases). Moreover, if any removal is tried and is taking too much time, it may require alternating it with the chest compressions at some moments, without hindering to the extraction. And, whether the object has been found and removed in this step or not, the CPR procedure must pass to the next step and continue until the victims can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

Rescue breaths of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

In the next step of the CPR, it is recommended that the rescuer applies a rescue breath, pinching the victim's nose and puffing air inside of the mouth. Rescue breaths would usually fail while the obstructing object is blocking the entrance of air. This can be resolved by tilting the victim's head up and down, thus altering the shape of the airway and attempting to open an entrance for the air, and then giving another rescue breath. After the rescue breaths, this resuscitation returns to the 30 initial compressions, in a cycle that repeats continually, until the victim regains consciousness and breathes,[51] or until the object is extracted.

Unconscious choking may lead to cardiac arrest, in which case defibrillation is needed.[52] It is convenient to ask around for a defibrillator, such as an AED, to be used on a victim that remains in cardiac arrest after having extracted the stuck object (if it has been extracted, and only after that). An AED is designed to be easy to use by an untrained person by guiding the user with voice instructions.

sources.section: Treatment › Particular cases › Infants (babies under 1 year-old) › Unconscious infants
sources.text:
Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in children less than one year old because they can cause liver damage.[59]

An unconscious infant has to be placed face-up on a firm and horizontal surface (as the floor). The baby's head must be in a straight position, facing frontally, because tilting it too much backwards can close the windpipe (trachea) in infants.

Emergency medical services should be summoned, and an automated external defibrillator (AED) should be retrieved.

Until emergency services arrive, the American Heart Association[59] recommends starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) adapted to infants (<1 year old). It is a cycle of resuscitation[60] that alternates compressions and rescue breaths, like in a normal CPR, but with some differences:
The rescuer begins by making 30 compressions, pressing, with two thumbs or the heel of one's hand, on the lower half of the bone in the middle of the chest (the sternum, on its part that is the nearest to the belly), at an approximate rate of nearly 2 per second (100-120 compressions per minute).

At the end of the round of compressions, the rescuer looks into the mouth for the obstructing object. And, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it (usually using a finger sweep). The rescuer must not confuse a foreign object with epiglottis: a cartilaginous flap of the throat, nor with uvula: a piece of flesh in the back of the mouth. Current protocols do not recommend attempting to extract the object if it is not visible (a blind extraction) because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident. In total, no more than ten seconds should be spent without doing compressions. If the object cannot be immediately extracted, this CPR procedure must continue to the next action and continue until the babies can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

In the next step of the CPR, the rescuer makes a rescue breath, covering the baby's mouth and nose simultaneously with their own mouth, and gently exhaling one time. The goal of a rescue breath is to observe the rise and fall of the chest, indicating that air has reached the lungs. However, one should be careful so as to not overinflate the baby's lungs; a rescuer should not attempt to blow against resistance. After two rescue breaths, the rescuer must return to the 30 initial compressions, repeating the same resuscitation cycle again, continually, until the choking baby regains consciousness and begins to breathe normally, or until emergency help arrives.

Defibrillation may be needed, as a choking infant that is already unconscious can suffer a cardiac arrest at any moment due to hypoxia.[52] AEDs, which are available in many public places, are designed to be safe and easy to use; they announce instructions with voice messages, and the device will not shock a patient who does not require defibrillation. One of the pads of the AED is attached to the baby's chest, and the other pad to the baby's back.

sources.original_text:
A choking victim who becomes unconscious[3][48][49] must be gently caught before falling and placed lying face-up on a surface.[50] That surface should be firm enough (it is recommended placing a layer of something on the floor and laying the victim above).

Emergency medical services should be summoned, if this has not already been done.

It can be also convenient that any rescuer asks for a defibrillator around (an AED, as those devices are commonplace), just in case it can be necessary to treat the victim's heart.

Chest compressions of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), proper rhythm.

The anti-choking cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for unconscious adults and children is quite similar to any other CPR, but with some modifications:

In a first step, a series of 30 chest compressions are applied on the lower half of the sternum (the bone that is along the middle of the chest from the neck to the belly) at an approximate rhythm of nearly 2 per second.

After that series, the rescuer looks for the obstructing object and, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it, usually by using a finger sweeping (hopefully from the mouth). Normally, the object would be a food bolus (and not the epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap of the throat). It is also possible to try to extract it when it is deeper and not visible, always carefully: using the fingers to take it, or lifting the victim's chin to form a straight way to the throat while the victim is face up (face down in case of the victim's tongue obstructs too much, or on a side with a base under the head) and then grasping or sweeping the stuck object with tools: thin kitchen tweezers, scissors (these used with care), forks and spoons (in a reverse position: introducing their handle) or even a toothpick (if other instruments were too big for the case); however, the protocols do not recommend extracting the obstructing object if it is not visible (a blind extraction), because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident, and because the compressions could move the object outside by themselves (in some cases). Moreover, if any removal is tried and is taking too much time, it may require alternating it with the chest compressions at some moments, without hindering to the extraction. And, whether the object has been found and removed in this step or not, the CPR procedure must pass to the next step and continue until the victims can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

Rescue breaths of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

In the next step of the CPR, it is recommended that the rescuer applies a rescue breath, pinching the victim's nose and puffing air inside of the mouth. Rescue breaths would usually fail while the obstructing object is blocking the entrance of air. This can be resolved by tilting the victim's head up and down, thus altering the shape of the airway and attempting to open an entrance for the air, and then giving another rescue breath. After the rescue breaths, this resuscitation returns to the 30 initial compressions, in a cycle that repeats continually, until the victim regains consciousness and breathes,[51] or until the object is extracted.

Unconscious choking may lead to cardiac arrest, in which case defibrillation is needed.[52] It is convenient to ask around for a defibrillator, such as an AED, to be used on a victim that remains in cardiac arrest after having extracted the stuck object (if it has been extracted, and only after that). An AED is designed to be easy to use by an untrained person by guiding the user with voice instructions.

**CRITICAL UPDATE: ADMINISTER SECOND DOSE IMMEDIATELY**

Your child's symptoms (wheezing and faintness) persisting 6 minutes after the first injection indicate that the reaction is not resolving. You must act immediately to reverse the airway swelling and drop in blood pressure.

**IMMEDIATE STEPS:**
1.  **Inject Second Epinephrine Dose NOW:**
    *   Use the second auto-injector immediately [S3].
    *   Inject into the **outer thigh**, even through clothing [S1].
    *   Hold for the specified time (usually 3 seconds) until the device clicks or releases [S1].
2.  **Position the Child:**
    *   Since she is wheezing and faint, keep her in the position that allows best breathing while supporting blood flow. If lying flat makes breathing worse, keep her sitting up slowly with shoulders raised; otherwise, lay her down with legs raised to prevent fainting [S3].
    *   **Do not** let her stand or walk [S3].
3.  **Call Emergency Services:**
    *   Dial your local emergency number immediately (e.g., 911) if you have not already done so, and report that the symptoms are worsening despite the first dose [S3].
4.  **Monitor Closely:**
    *   Watch for improvement in breathing or consciousness over the next few minutes. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing, begin CPR if trained [S1].

**Why this is urgent:**
*   The guidelines state that if symptoms persist after 5–15 minutes without improvement, a second dose should be administered [S1][S3].
*   Persistent wheezing and faintness are signs of ongoing airway obstruction and low blood pressure (shock), which epinephrine is the only medication to treat effectively in this acute phase [S1].

**Not backed by local sources (General Knowledge):**
*   **Antihistamines are not the priority:** Even if you have antihistamine tablets, they do not replace epinephrine and will not fix the throat swelling or wheezing quickly enough to save her life. They should only be given later if she is stable [S1][S5].
*   **Steroids are not immediate treatment:** Oral steroids (like prednisone) take hours to work and do not help with the current breathing crisis [S5].

**WARNING SIGNS & PROFESSIONAL HELP:**
*   **Warning Signs:** Continued wheezing, difficulty swallowing, blue lips/fingernails, or unconsciousness indicate critical failure of airway or circulation [S1].
*   **Seek Professional Help:** This is a life-threatening emergency requiring hospital transport immediately. A biphasic reaction (return of symptoms after initial improvement) can occur, making the second dose crucial even if she seems to improve slightly later [S6].

**Summary:** Give 2nd epinephrine NOW → Keep her safe from falling/fainting → Call Emergency Services → Transport to hospital.

sources.title: Anaphylaxis
sources.text:
People prone to anaphylaxis are advised to have an allergy action plan. Parents are advised to inform schools of their children's allergies and what to do in case of an anaphylactic emergency. The action plan usually includes use of epinephrine autoinjectors, the recommendation to wear a medical alert bracelet, and counseling on avoidance of triggers.[68] Immunotherapy is available for certain triggers to prevent future episodes of anaphylaxis. A multi-year course of subcutaneous desensitization has been found effective against stinging insects, while oral desensitization is effective for many foods.[16]

In July 2026, the United Kingdom passed Benedict's Law an amendment to the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 which requires every school in England to hold spare adrenaline auto-injectors and provide compulsory allergy training for all staff.[69]

sources.text: Antihistamines (both H1 and H2), while commonly used and assumed effective based on theoretical reasoning, are poorly supported by evidence.[66][67] A 2007 Cochrane review did not find any good-quality studies upon which to base recommendations[67] and they are not believed to affect airway edema or spasm.[10] Corticosteroids are unlikely to make a difference in the current episode of anaphylaxis, but may be used in the hope of decreasing the risk of biphasic anaphylaxis. Their prophylactic effectiveness in these situations is uncertain.[55] Nebulized salbutamol may be effective for bronchospasm that does not resolve with epinephrine.[10] Methylene blue has been used in those not responsive to other measures due to its presumed effect of relaxing smooth muscle.[10]

sources.text:
Biphasic reactions are rare and can occur anywhere from 10 minutes up to six days after an initial reaction.[2]

- Uniphasic response, followed by asymptomatic period of hour or more, then return of symptoms
- The second phase does not necessarily resemble the first!
- More likely with a severe initial presentation, hypotension, and recurrent epinephrine dosing requirements in the emergency department[3]
- Little evidence to support the use of discharge steroids to prevent a biphasic reaction
- 0.4% of patients with anaphylaxis had a rebound event while in the ED[4]

This is a life-threatening emergency. Act immediately based on the baby's responsiveness.

**Scenario A: The baby is still responsive (conscious, moving)**
*Note: If the baby is turning blue, they are in severe distress and may become unresponsive at any second.*

1.  **Call for help:** Shout for someone else to call emergency services immediately.
2.  **Position the baby:** Hold the baby face down on your forearm with their head lower than their chest. Support the jaw gently [S1].
3.  **Give back blows:** Deliver up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand [S1][S4].
4.  **Check and repeat:** If nothing is expelled, turn the baby face up while keeping the head lower than the chest [S1].
5.  **Give chest thrusts:** Place two fingers on the center of the breastbone (sternum) and push down firmly about 4 cm [S2][S4].
6.  **Repeat cycle:** Alternate between 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the baby becomes unresponsive [S1][S4].
7.  **Stop criteria:** Stop only if the baby starts breathing normally, coughing forcefully, or crying [S1].

**Scenario B: The baby becomes unresponsive (stops moving/crying)**
*If the baby loses consciousness during the process:*

1.  **Stop choking maneuvers:** Lay the baby on their back on a firm, flat surface immediately [S2].
2.  **Call emergency services:** If not already done, call emergency services and put the phone on speakerphone [S2].
3.  **Start Infant CPR:** Begin chest compressions. Place two fingers in the center of the breastbone and press down about 4 cm at a rate of 100–120 per minute [S2].
4.  **Rescue breaths:** After 30 compressions, give 2 gentle rescue breaths (seal mouth over baby's nose and mouth, blow for 1 second until chest rises) [S2].
5.  **Remove visible objects only:** Only remove an object if you can see it clearly in the mouth; do not perform blind finger sweeps [S2].
6.  **Continue CPR:** Repeat the cycle of 30 compressions and 2 breaths until normal breathing returns or professional help takes over [S2].

**Critical Safety Warnings**
*   **Do NOT use abdominal thrusts (Heimlich):** These can cause liver damage in infants under 1 year old [S4].
*   **Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps:** This can push the object deeper into the airway [S1].
*   **Head position:** Always keep the head neutral or lower than the chest during interventions to prevent aspiration, but do not tilt the head backward excessively [S2][S4].

*This guidance is based on standard first aid protocols found in offline sources. It does not replace professional medical training or advice from a doctor.*

sources.text:
The majority of choking injuries and fatalities occur in children aged 0–4,[56] highlighting the importance for widespread dissemination of the appropriate anti-choking techniques for these age groups. In fact, it has been shown that increased parental education may decrease choking rates among children.[57]

For infants under 1 year-old, the American Heart Association recommends adapted procedures.[58] The size of the children's body is the most important aspect in determining the correct anti-choking technique. So the normal first aid techniques against choking would be tried in children who are too large for the babies' procedures (or they would be tried as a less appropriated attempt if the rescuer is unable to perform the techniques for babies).

First aid for choking infants alternates a cycle of special back blows (five back slaps) followed by special chest thrusts (five adapted chest compressions).

Left:

'Back blows for infants', the baby receives the slaps being carefully held and slightly placed upside-down; a support under the chest is recommended.

Right:

'Chest thrusts for infants', two fingers press on the lower half of the middle of the chest.

In the back blows maneuver, the rescuer slaps on the baby's back. It is recommended that the baby receive them being slightly leaned upside-down on an inclination. There exist several ways to achieve this:

According to a widely propagated modality: the rescuer sits down on a seat with the baby, and supports the baby with a forearm and its respective hand. The baby's head must be carefully held with that hand (approximately by the face), and kept in a normal position, facing forward, not inclinated. Then the baby's body can be leaned forward upside-down along the rescuer's thighs, and receive the slaps.

As an easier alternative: the rescuer can sit on a bed or sofa, or even the floor, carrying the baby. Next, the rescuer should support the baby's body on the own lap, to lean the baby a bit upside-down at the right or the left of the lap. The baby's head must be in a normal position, facing forward, frontally, and not inclinated. It is always convenient that the baby's chest is supported against something. Then the rescuer would slap the back of the baby.

If the rescuer cannot sit down: at least it is possible to attempt the manoeuver at a low height and over a soft surface. Then the rescuer would support the baby with a forearm and the hand of that side, holding carefully the baby's head with that hand (approximately by the face, but always trying that the baby's head keeps in a normal position, facing forward, not inclinated). The baby's body would be leaned upside-down in that position to receive the slaps. In situations with rescuers who cannot do all of that (as rescuers with disabilities and others), they can still try the normal back blows, supporting the baby's chest with one hand, bending the baby's body, and then giving firm slaps with the other hand.

In the chest thrusts manoeuver, the baby's body is placed lying face up on a surface (it can be the rescuer's thighs, lap or forearm). Then, the rescuer does the compressions pressing with only two fingers on the lower half of the bone that is along the middle of the chest from the neck to the belly (on the chest bone, named sternum, on its part that is the nearest to the belly). Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in children less than one year old because they can cause liver damage.[59]

The back blows and chest thrusts are alternated in cycles of five back blows and five chest compressions until the object comes out of the infant's airway or until the infant becomes unconscious.[59]

If choking is unresolved despite these rescue attempts, it is vital that somebody calls to the emergency medical services and continue first aid until they arrive. An infant can fall unconscious soon, then an anti-choking resuscitation for infants is required (read next).

sources.original_text:
All young children require care in eating, and they must learn to chew their food completely to avoid choking. Feeding them while they are running, playing, laughing, etc. increases the risk of choking. Caregivers must supervise children while eating or playing.[70]

Pediatricians and dentists can provide information on various age groups to parents and caregivers about which food and toys are appropriate to prevent choking.[17]

Little children can choke on any type of plastic bag or plastic balloon, as the bags for diapers

It is recommended waiting until 6 months of age before introducing solid foods to infants (according to the American Academy of Pediatricians).[71] Caregivers should avoid giving children younger than 5 years-old foods that pose a high risk of choking, such as hot dog pieces, bananas, cheese sticks, cheese chunks, hard candy, nuts, grapes, marshmallows, or popcorn.[70] Later, when they are accustomed to these foods, it is recommended to serve them split into small pieces. Some foods as hot dogs, bananas, or grapes are usually split lengthwise, sliced, or both (being the cut into slices the main part for safety in many long-shaped foods).[17]

Children readily put small objects into their mouths (deflated balloons, marbles, small pieces, buttons, coins, button batteries, etc.), which can lead to choking. A complicated obstruction for babies is choking on deflated balloons (including preservatives) or plastic bags. This also includes the nappy sacks, used for wrapping the dirty diapers, which are sometimes dangerously placed near the babies.[72] To prevent children from swallowing things, precautions should be taken in the environment to keep dangerous objects out of their reach. Small children must be supervised closely and taught to avoid putting things into their mouths. Toys and games may indicate on their packages the ages for which they are safe. In the US, children's toy and product manufacturers are required by law to apply appropriate warning labels to their packaging,[17] but toys that are resold may not have them.[17] Caregivers can try to prevent choking by considering the features of a toy (such as size, shape, consistency and small parts) before giving it to a child.[17] Children's products that are found to pose a choking risk can be taken off the market.[17]

Parents, teachers, and other caregivers for children are advised to be trained in choking first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

**IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED:** Your baby is unresponsive, not breathing, and turning blue. This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call Emergency Services (911, 112, or your local number) immediately** if you can still reach the phone. Put the phone on speaker so you can follow instructions while acting.

Here are the exact steps to take right now:

### Step 1: Call for Help
*   Dial emergency services immediately.
*   State clearly: "My baby is choking, unconscious, and not breathing."
*   Follow the dispatcher's instructions exactly.

### Step 2: Check Safety and Position
*   Ensure the scene is safe for you (no fire, electricity, etc.).
*   Place the infant on a **firm, flat surface** (like the floor), face up. Do not use a soft bed or couch. [S3]
*   Keep the baby's head in a **straight, neutral position**. Do not tilt the head back too much, as this can close the airway in infants. [S3]

### Step 3: Start Infant CPR (30 Compressions)
Since you have no prior training and the baby is unresponsive, begin with compressions immediately.
*   **Hand Placement:** Place two fingers (index and middle) or the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone/sternum). [S2]
*   **Technique:** Press down hard and fast.
    *   **Depth:** About 4 cm (1.5 inches). [S2]
    *   **Rate:** 100 to 120 compressions per minute (about 2 presses per second). [S3]
    *   **Recoil:** Allow the chest to fully rise after each press; do not lean on the baby. [S2]
*   Perform **30 compressions** continuously.

### Step 4: Check for Object (Do Not Blindly Sweep)
*   After 30 compressions, look into the baby's mouth briefly.
*   **ONLY** remove an object if it is clearly visible and easy to grab. [S2]
*   **DO NOT** perform blind finger sweeps or try to dig for the object, as this can push it deeper. [S3]
*   If you cannot see the object quickly (within 10 seconds), stop checking and return to compressions immediately.

### Step 5: Give Rescue Breaths
*   **Seal:** Place your mouth over the baby's mouth and nose simultaneously.
*   **Exhale:** Gently blow for about **1 second**.
*   **Check:** Watch for the chest to rise. Do not force air if you feel resistance. [S3]
*   Give **2 rescue breaths**.

### Step 6: Repeat Cycle
*   Continue the cycle of **30 compressions** followed by **2 rescue breaths**.
*   Keep going until:
    *   The baby starts breathing normally or wakes up.
    *   Emergency help arrives and takes over.
    *   You are physically unable to continue.

### Critical Safety Warnings
*   **No Abdominal Thrusts:** Do not perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) on an infant under 1 year old; this can cause severe internal injury like liver damage. [S3]
*   **Do Not Lose Time:** If the object is not visible, do not spend more than 10 seconds searching; resume compressions immediately. [S3]
*   **AED Use:** If an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) is available, turn it on and follow its voice prompts. Pads are placed on the chest and back for infants. [S3]

**Not backed by local sources:**

*   Do not stop CPR even if you see the object; the lack of breathing indicates heart/lung failure which requires circulation support first.

sources.text: If a choking baby under 1 year becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, stop choking maneuvers, call emergency services on speakerphone and start infant CPR on a firm, flat surface. For a single rescuer, encircle the chest with both hands, thumbs on the breastbone’s center; give 30 compressions about 4 cm deep at 100–120 per minute, allowing recoil. sources.text:
Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in children less than one year old because they can cause liver damage.[59]

An unconscious infant has to be placed face-up on a firm and horizontal surface (as the floor). The baby's head must be in a straight position, facing frontally, because tilting it too much backwards can close the windpipe (trachea) in infants.

Emergency medical services should be summoned, and an automated external defibrillator (AED) should be retrieved.

Until emergency services arrive, the American Heart Association[59] recommends starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) adapted to infants (<1 year old). It is a cycle of resuscitation[60] that alternates compressions and rescue breaths, like in a normal CPR, but with some differences:
The rescuer begins by making 30 compressions, pressing, with two thumbs or the heel of one's hand, on the lower half of the bone in the middle of the chest (the sternum, on its part that is the nearest to the belly), at an approximate rate of nearly 2 per second (100-120 compressions per minute).

At the end of the round of compressions, the rescuer looks into the mouth for the obstructing object. And, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it (usually using a finger sweep). The rescuer must not confuse a foreign object with epiglottis: a cartilaginous flap of the throat, nor with uvula: a piece of flesh in the back of the mouth. Current protocols do not recommend attempting to extract the object if it is not visible (a blind extraction) because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident. In total, no more than ten seconds should be spent without doing compressions. If the object cannot be immediately extracted, this CPR procedure must continue to the next action and continue until the babies can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

In the next step of the CPR, the rescuer makes a rescue breath, covering the baby's mouth and nose simultaneously with their own mouth, and gently exhaling one time. The goal of a rescue breath is to observe the rise and fall of the chest, indicating that air has reached the lungs. However, one should be careful so as to not overinflate the baby's lungs; a rescuer should not attempt to blow against resistance. After two rescue breaths, the rescuer must return to the 30 initial compressions, repeating the same resuscitation cycle again, continually, until the choking baby regains consciousness and begins to breathe normally, or until emergency help arrives.

Defibrillation may be needed, as a choking infant that is already unconscious can suffer a cardiac arrest at any moment due to hypoxia.[52] AEDs, which are available in many public places, are designed to be safe and easy to use; they announce instructions with voice messages, and the device will not shock a patient who does not require defibrillation. One of the pads of the AED is attached to the baby's chest, and the other pad to the baby's back.

sources.original_text:
A choking victim who becomes unconscious[3][48][49] must be gently caught before falling and placed lying face-up on a surface.[50] That surface should be firm enough (it is recommended placing a layer of something on the floor and laying the victim above).

Emergency medical services should be summoned, if this has not already been done.

It can be also convenient that any rescuer asks for a defibrillator around (an AED, as those devices are commonplace), just in case it can be necessary to treat the victim's heart.

Chest compressions of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), proper rhythm.

The anti-choking cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for unconscious adults and children is quite similar to any other CPR, but with some modifications:

In a first step, a series of 30 chest compressions are applied on the lower half of the sternum (the bone that is along the middle of the chest from the neck to the belly) at an approximate rhythm of nearly 2 per second.

After that series, the rescuer looks for the obstructing object and, if it is already visible, the rescuer makes a try to extract it, usually by using a finger sweeping (hopefully from the mouth). Normally, the object would be a food bolus (and not the epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap of the throat). It is also possible to try to extract it when it is deeper and not visible, always carefully: using the fingers to take it, or lifting the victim's chin to form a straight way to the throat while the victim is face up (face down in case of the victim's tongue obstructs too much, or on a side with a base under the head) and then grasping or sweeping the stuck object with tools: thin kitchen tweezers, scissors (these used with care), forks and spoons (in a reverse position: introducing their handle) or even a toothpick (if other instruments were too big for the case); however, the protocols do not recommend extracting the obstructing object if it is not visible (a blind extraction), because of the risk to sink it deeper by accident, and because the compressions could move the object outside by themselves (in some cases). Moreover, if any removal is tried and is taking too much time, it may require alternating it with the chest compressions at some moments, without hindering to the extraction. And, whether the object has been found and removed in this step or not, the CPR procedure must pass to the next step and continue until the victims can breathe by themselves or emergency medical services arrive.

Rescue breaths of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

In the next step of the CPR, it is recommended that the rescuer applies a rescue breath, pinching the victim's nose and puffing air inside of the mouth. Rescue breaths would usually fail while the obstructing object is blocking the entrance of air. This can be resolved by tilting the victim's head up and down, thus altering the shape of the airway and attempting to open an entrance for the air, and then giving another rescue breath. After the rescue breaths, this resuscitation returns to the 30 initial compressions, in a cycle that repeats continually, until the victim regains consciousness and breathes,[51] or until the object is extracted.

Unconscious choking may lead to cardiac arrest, in which case defibrillation is needed.[52] It is convenient to ask around for a defibrillator, such as an AED, to be used on a victim that remains in cardiac arrest after having extracted the stuck object (if it has been extracted, and only after that). An AED is designed to be easy to use by an untrained person by guiding the user with voice instructions.

validation_inputs.draft:
**DO NOT wait for an antihistamine.** This situation describes severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). Antihistamines help with itching but **do not replace** epinephrine and do not treat airway swelling or shock [S1].

Follow these steps immediately:

1.  **Inject Epinephrine Immediately**: Use the prescribed epinephrine auto-injector in the **outer thigh**, even through clothing [S1].
2.  **Position the Child**: Lay her down with legs raised. If she is having severe shortness of breath, allow her to sit up slowly; do not let her stand or walk [S3].
3.  **Call Emergency Services**: Call your local emergency number right away [S3].
4.  **Monitor and Repeat**: If symptoms do not improve after 5–15 minutes and a second dose is available, administer a second auto-injector [S1][S3].
5.  **Do Not Rely on Antihistamines**: While antihistamine tablets can help with itching, they are not effective for airway edema or spasm and must never delay epinephrine administration [S1][S5].

**Warning Signs & Professional Help**:
*   Symptoms like a swollen tongue, wheezing, and faintness indicate life-threatening airway obstruction and circulatory collapse.
*   This does not replace a doctor's care; professional medical help is required immediately.
*   Biphasic reactions (return of symptoms) can occur 10 minutes to six days after the initial reaction, so continued monitoring is necessary [S6].

**Not backed by local sources**:
*   Keep the child calm and warm while waiting for emergency services.
*   If vomiting occurs while lying down, roll her onto her side to prevent choking.

- Antihistamine tablets help with itching, but **do not replace** epinephrine.

sources.text:
People prone to anaphylaxis are advised to have an allergy action plan. Parents are advised to inform schools of their children's allergies and what to do in case of an anaphylactic emergency. The action plan usually includes use of epinephrine autoinjectors, the recommendation to wear a medical alert bracelet, and counseling on avoidance of triggers.[68] Immunotherapy is available for certain triggers to prevent future episodes of anaphylaxis. A multi-year course of subcutaneous desensitization has been found effective against stinging insects, while oral desensitization is effective for many foods.[16]

In July 2026, the United Kingdom passed Benedict's Law an amendment to the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 which requires every school in England to hold spare adrenaline auto-injectors and provide compulsory allergy training for all staff.[69]

sources.text: Antihistamines (both H1 and H2), while commonly used and assumed effective based on theoretical reasoning, are poorly supported by evidence.[66][67] A 2007 Cochrane review did not find any good-quality studies upon which to base recommendations[67] and they are not believed to affect airway edema or spasm.[10] Corticosteroids are unlikely to make a difference in the current episode of anaphylaxis, but may be used in the hope of decreasing the risk of biphasic anaphylaxis. sources.text:
Biphasic reactions are rare and can occur anywhere from 10 minutes up to six days after an initial reaction.[2]

- Uniphasic response, followed by asymptomatic period of hour or more, then return of symptoms
- The second phase does not necessarily resemble the first!
- More likely with a severe initial presentation, hypotension, and recurrent epinephrine dosing requirements in the emergency department[3]
- Little evidence to support the use of discharge steroids to prevent a biphasic reaction
- 0.4% of patients with anaphylaxis had a rebound event while in the ED[4]

sources.text:
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, shortness of breath, wheezing, widespread hives, dizziness or fainting after an insect sting, food or medicine.

- Use an **epinephrine (adrenaline) auto-injector** (if the person has one) in the outer thigh, even through clothing. It can be repeated in 5–15 min if there is no improvement and a second dose is available.
- Lay the person down with legs raised (or sitting if shortness of breath is worse).
- Antihistamine tablets help with itching, but **do not replace** epinephrine.

> Source: World Allergy Organization — *Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020*; IFRC 2020.

validation_inputs.draft:
**Immediate Action Required**

1.  **Use the second epinephrine auto-injector immediately.**
    *   Symptoms persisting 5 minutes after the first dose indicate the reaction is not resolving. You should administer a second dose in the outer thigh, even through clothing [S1].
    *   Ensure she is lying down with legs raised (or sitting up slowly if breathing is difficult; do not let her stand or walk) while administering the second shot [S3].

2.  **Call Emergency Services.**
    *   Continue to monitor her breathing and consciousness closely. Even after treatment, symptoms can return (biphasic reaction), though this is less common than the initial severity determining risk [S6].

**What NOT to do:**
*   **Do not wait for an antihistamine.** Antihistamines help with itching but **do not replace epinephrine** and are poorly supported by evidence for treating airway swelling or breathing spasms in anaphylaxis [S1][S5]. They should not delay or substitute the use of a second epinephrine dose.

**Not backed by local sources:**
*   If she remains wheezing after the second epinephrine injection and cannot breathe adequately, emergency medical services may be required to provide advanced airway management or nebulized bronchodilators (like salbutamol) in a hospital setting [S5].
*   Monitor for signs of a biphasic reaction: symptoms returning after an initial improvement period can occur 10 minutes to several days later, especially with severe initial presentations [S6].

⚠️ **Warning:** This situation is life-threatening. Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment that reverses airway swelling and shock. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you are trained to do so. Do not hesitate to seek professional help immediately.

No, your family cannot use the well water until it is confirmed safe. The smell of gasoline indicates chemical contamination (fuel), which boiling or disinfecting **cannot** remove [S1][S2]. You must obtain a different safe supply immediately.

Here are the steps to take:

1.  **Stop using the well water immediately.** Do not drink, cook with, or use it for washing if ingestion is possible.
2.  **Use sealed bottled water.** Switch entirely to bottled water or another verified safe source until the contamination is resolved [S2].
3.  **Contact local health authorities.** Report the gasoline smell and flooding to your local public-health department for specific advice on how to decontaminate or permanently close the well [S1][S2].
4.  **Do not attempt to treat the water yourself.** Fuel and toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling, filtering with cloth/filters, or adding bleach [S1][S2].

**Why bottled water is the correct choice here:**
*   The CDC explicitly states that water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting; you must obtain a different safe supply [S1].
*   Adding disinfectant (like bleach) only kills germs; it does not remove chemical toxins like gasoline [S2].

**Not backed by local sources:**
*   **Chemical Contamination Risks:** Gasoline is toxic and flammable. Ingesting water with fuel can cause nausea, vomiting, headache, or more severe poisoning depending on the amount. Inhalation of fumes is also dangerous.
*   **Flooding Context:** Flooding often mixes surface runoff (which may contain gasoline from vehicles) with groundwater sources like wells. Even if no one is ill yet, the chemical presence remains a threat until verified by testing or official closure.

**Summary Action:** Discard any water drawn from that well. Use only sealed bottled water until local authorities confirm the well is safe or advise on permanent remediation.

sources.section: Boiling cloudy drinking water: chemical contamination and elevation limits
sources.text:
Follow local public-health advice about the water supply. Use safe bottled water if available. Water contaminated with fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting it; obtain a different safe supply.

When the concern is germs and safe bottled water is unavailable, first pass cloudy water through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter, or allow it to settle and draw off the clear water. Bring the clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 6,500 feet elevation, boil for 3 minutes. Let it cool and store it in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.

This boiling summary does not provide a bleach dose; product ingredients and concentration must be known before using a product-specific disinfection procedure.

Source: [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html) — Water with fuel or toxic chemicals in it; Steps for boiling water; companion one-page fact sheet. Edition: Supporting page September 19, 2024; fact-sheet listing August 28, 2024. Scope: General public. Region: United States source; follow local public-health advice.

School lessons - Background information

         Water contamination at the source

              Water can already be contaminated at the source. Especially in surface waters the risk of
              water contamination is very high. Groundwater is usually much purer than surface water
              but may be contaminated by natural chemicals or by anthropogenic activities. Rainwater
              harvested from sheet or tile roofs is relatively pure, particularly if the first water after a dry
              period is discarded or allowed to run off to waste.
              Improved drinking water sources are defined in terms of the type of technology and
              level of service most likely to provide safe water than unimproved technologies. Improved
              water sources include household connections, public standpipes, boreholes, protected
              dug wells, protected springs, and rainwater collection. Unimproved water sources are
              unprotected wells or springs.
              Actions to protect water sources:
              • regularly cleaning of the area around the water source
              • moving latrines away from and downstream of water sources (30 m)
              • building fences to prevent animals from getting into open water sources
              • lining wells to prevent surface water from contaminating the groundwater
              • building proper drainage for wastewater around taps and wells10

School lessons

Key messages of the lesson

• Water contamination can occur at the source, during transport or through
    inaccurate storage.

• Improvement of the water quality is one barrier for disease transmission.
• Turbid water is normally unsafe, but also clear water can be contaminated.

Safe water

Materials: Drawing material
Image: A look into water
1. Explain the differences between safe and unsafe water.

      –– Water contains very small organisms like bacteria and viruses that are invisible to the
           human eye. Some of the small organisms pose a severe threat to human health as they
           cause different diseases with the following symptoms: vomiting, stomach pain or diarrhoea.

      –– Turbid water is normally unsafe, but also clear water can be contaminated.
      –– Safe water is free from disease-causing organisms and harmful chemical substances.
2. Let the children draw their vision of the small organisms contaminating the water.
    Show them the image “A look into water” as an example.

                                                        A look into water

**Immediate Action Plan for Hypoglycemia (Glucose < 70 mg/dL)**

1.  **Verify Status**: Confirm your husband is fully awake and can swallow safely. Since he meets these criteria, proceed with oral treatment. [S1], [S5]
2.  **Administer Fast-Acting Carbohydrate**: Have him drink the juice immediately. Aim for approximately **1/2 cup (~120 mL)** of regular juice (not diet). This provides roughly 15–15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate. [S1], [S5]
    *   *Note*: Glucose tablets or gel are often cited as more effective, but juice is a valid alternative if those are unavailable. [S5]
3.  **Wait and Recheck**: Wait exactly **15 minutes**. Do not give more food during this time. [S1], [S5]
4.  **Re-measure Glucose**: Check his blood sugar level again.
    *   **If still below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)**: Repeat Step 2 with another 1/2 cup of juice or 15 grams of another fast-acting carb, then wait 15 minutes again. [S1], [S5]
    *   **If above 70 mg/dL**: He has recovered from the immediate crisis.
5.  **Prevent Recurrence**: Once his blood sugar is normal, have him eat a small snack or meal containing both **carbohydrate and protein** (e.g., crackers with cheese, peanut butter sandwich) to stabilize levels and replenish glycogen stores. [S1], [S5]

**Warning Signs & When to Seek Help**
*   **Do NOT give anything by mouth** if he becomes unconscious, confused enough to risk choking, or unable to swallow safely. In such cases, call emergency services immediately. [S2]
*   If he does not improve after two rounds of the 15-15 rule (30 minutes total), or if symptoms worsen, seek emergency medical help. [S2], [S5]

**General Diabetes Management Context**
*   Long-term management focuses on keeping blood sugar close to normal levels through diet, exercise, and medication to prevent complications. [S4]
*   Annual foot examinations are recommended for people with diabetes to check sensation and structure, as high or low blood sugar can affect foot health. [S4]

***Disclaimer**: This information is based on standard first-aid guidelines and does not replace professional medical advice. Always follow specific instructions from a healthcare provider regarding your husband's condition.*

sources.section: How to treat severe low blood sugar
sources.text: If low blood sugar causes unconsciousness, do not give anything by mouth. If unresponsive or unable to swallow safely, seek emergency help. If unresponsive and breathing normally, place them on their side in the recovery position. If unconscious with severe low blood sugar, use available glucagon only if you know how. Stay with them and monitor breathing.

sources.title: Hypoglycemia
sources.text:
See also:

Glucose-elevating agent

After hypoglycemia in a person is identified, rapid treatment is necessary and can be life-saving.[1] The main goal of treatment is to raise blood glucose back to normal levels, which is done through various ways of administering glucose, depending on the severity of the hypoglycemia, what is on-hand to treat, and who is administering the treatment.[1][3] A general rule used by the American Diabetes Association is the "15-15 Rule," which suggests consuming or administering 15 grams of a carbohydrate, followed by a 15-minute wait and re-measurement of blood glucose level to assess if blood glucose has returned to normal levels.[5]

sources.title: Diabetes
sources.text:
Main article:

Diabetes management

Diabetes management concentrates on keeping blood sugar levels close to normal, without causing low blood sugar.[121] This can usually be accomplished with dietary changes,[122] exercise, weight loss, and use of appropriate medications (insulin, oral medications).[121]

Learning about the disease and actively participating in the treatment is important, since complications are far less common and less severe in people who have well-managed blood sugar levels.[121][123] The goal of treatment is an HbA1C level below 7%.[124][125] Attention is also paid to other health problems that may accelerate the negative effects of diabetes. These include smoking, high blood pressure, metabolic syndrome, obesity, and lack of regular exercise.[121][126] Specialized footwear is widely used to reduce the risk of diabetic foot ulcers by relieving the pressure on the foot.[127][128][129] Foot examination for patients living with diabetes should be done annually which includes sensation testing, foot biomechanics, vascular integrity and foot structure.[130]

Concerning those with severe mental illness, the efficacy of type 2 diabetes self-management interventions is still poorly explored, with insufficient scientific evidence to show whether these interventions have similar results to those observed in the general population.[131]

sources.title: Hypoglycemia
sources.text:
If an individual recognizes the symptoms of hypoglycemia coming on, blood sugar should promptly be measured, and a sugary food or drink should be consumed.[1] The person must be conscious and able to swallow.[1][3] The goal is to consume 10–20 grams of a carbohydrate to raise blood glucose levels to a minimum of 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).[3][2]

Examples of products to consume are:

- Glucose tabs or gel (refer to instructions on packet)[1][2]
- Juice containing sugar like apple, grape, or cranberry juice, 1/2 cup (~120 mL)[1][2]
- Soda or a soft-drink, 1/2 cup (~120 mL) (not diet soda)[2]
- Candy[2]
- Table sugar or honey, 1 tbsp (15 mL)[1]

Improvement in blood sugar levels and symptoms are expected to occur in 15–20 minutes, at which point blood sugar should be measured again.[3][2] If the repeat blood sugar level is not above 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), consume another 10–20 grams of a carbohydrate and remeasure blood sugar levels after 15–20 minutes.[3][2] Repeat until blood glucose levels have returned to normal levels.[3][2] After correcting blood glucose levels, people may consume a full meal within one hour to replenish glycogen stores.[2]

Among common monosaccharides and disaccharides, glucose (e.g. glucose syrup) and sucrose (table sugar, e.g. some candy) are more effective than fructose (e.g. apple concentrate, honey) in treating hypoglycemia. These two sugars have a higher glycemic index than fructose.[34] According to a 2017 meta-analysis, glucose tablets (GT) are 12% more likely to be effective within 15 minutes compared to dietary sources of sugar. Among the other pooled analyses, GT is not statistically significantly different from sucrose in effectiveness and is 21% more likely to be effective than orange juice. The meta-analysis also catalogs a number of RCTs dealing with other sugar sources along with their carbohydrate composition.[35]

A 2019 systematic review suggests, based on very limited evidence, that oral administration (swallowing) of glucose (tabs) leads to a bigger improvement in blood glucose levels when compared to buccal administration (dextrose gel).[36] This same review reported that, based on limited evidence, no difference was found in plasma glucose when administering combined oral and buccal glucose compared to only oral administration.[36] In the very specific setting of children with concomitant malaria or respiratory tract infection, sublingual administration of sucrose (table sugar) may be more effective than oral administration. This entails dissolving the table sugar under the tongue.[36]

After hypoglycemia in a person is identified, rapid treatment is necessary and can be life-saving.[1] The main goal of treatment is to raise blood glucose back to normal levels, which is done through various ways of administering glucose, depending on the severity of the hypoglycemia, what is on-hand to treat, and who is administering the treatment.[1][3] A general rule used by the American Diabetes Association is the "15-15 Rule," which suggests consuming or administering 15 grams of a carbohydrate, followed by a 15-minute wait and re-measurement of blood glucose level to assess if blood glucose has returned to normal levels.[5]

sources.title: Diabetes
sources.text:
Main article:

Diabetes management

Diabetes management concentrates on keeping blood sugar levels close to normal, without causing low blood sugar.[121] This can usually be accomplished with dietary changes,[122] exercise, weight loss, and use of appropriate medications (insulin, oral medications).[121]

Learning about the disease and actively participating in the treatment is important, since complications are far less common and less severe in people who have well-managed blood sugar levels.[121][123] The goal of treatment is an HbA1C level below 7%.[124][125] Attention is also paid to other health problems that may accelerate the negative effects of diabetes. These include smoking, high blood pressure, metabolic syndrome, obesity, and lack of regular exercise.[121][126] Specialized footwear is widely used to reduce the risk of diabetic foot ulcers by relieving the pressure on the foot.[127][128][129] Foot examination for patients living with diabetes should be done annually which includes sensation testing, foot biomechanics, vascular integrity and foot structure.[130]

Concerning those with severe mental illness, the efficacy of type 2 diabetes self-management interventions is still poorly explored, with insufficient scientific evidence to show whether these interventions have similar results to those observed in the general population.[131]

sources.title: Hypoglycemia
sources.text:
If an individual recognizes the symptoms of hypoglycemia coming on, blood sugar should promptly be measured, and a sugary food or drink should be consumed.[1] The person must be conscious and able to swallow.[1][3] The goal is to consume 10–20 grams of a carbohydrate to raise blood glucose levels to a minimum of 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).[3][2]

Examples of products to consume are:

- Glucose tabs or gel (refer to instructions on packet)[1][2]
- Juice containing sugar like apple, grape, or cranberry juice, 1/2 cup (~120 mL)[1][2]
- Soda or a soft-drink, 1/2 cup (~120 mL) (not diet soda)[2]
- Candy[2]
- Table sugar or honey, 1 tbsp (15 mL)[1]

Improvement in blood sugar levels and symptoms are expected to occur in 15–20 minutes, at which point blood sugar should be measured again.[3][2] If the repeat blood sugar level is not above 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), consume another 10–20 grams of a carbohydrate and remeasure blood sugar levels after 15–20 minutes.[3][2] Repeat until blood glucose levels have returned to normal levels.[3][2] After correcting blood glucose levels, people may consume a full meal within one hour to replenish glycogen stores.[2]

Among common monosaccharides and disaccharides, glucose (e.g. glucose syrup) and sucrose (table sugar, e.g. some candy) are more effective than fructose (e.g. apple concentrate, honey) in treating hypoglycemia. These two sugars have a higher glycemic index than fructose.[34] According to a 2017 meta-analysis, glucose tablets (GT) are 12% more likely to be effective within 15 minutes compared to dietary sources of sugar. Among the other pooled analyses, GT is not statistically significantly different from sucrose in effectiveness and is 21% more likely to be effective than orange juice. The meta-analysis also catalogs a number of RCTs dealing with other sugar sources along with their carbohydrate composition.[35]

A 2019 systematic review suggests, based on very limited evidence, that oral administration (swallowing) of glucose (tabs) leads to a bigger improvement in blood glucose levels when compared to buccal administration (dextrose gel).[36] This same review reported that, based on limited evidence, no difference was found in plasma glucose when administering combined oral and buccal glucose compared to only oral administration.[36] In the very specific setting of children with concomitant malaria or respiratory tract infection, sublingual administration of sucrose (table sugar) may be more effective than oral administration. This entails dissolving the table sugar under the tongue.[36]

No. Do not start chest compressions.

**Reason:**
*   Chest compressions are **only** performed if a person is **unresponsive** AND **not breathing normally** (cardiac arrest) [S1].
*   Your father is awake, talking clearly, and breathing normally, which means he does **not** meet the criteria for CPR [S2].
*   Starting CPR on someone who is conscious and breathing can cause serious harm, including broken ribs or internal injury [S4].

**Recommended Action:**
1.  **Ensure Safety:** Briefly check that the scene is safe (e.g., no fire, traffic, or electrical hazards) [S6].
2.  **Recovery Position:** If he was lying down and is now awake, you can keep him sitting or resting comfortably. If he becomes unconscious again but is still breathing normally, place him in the **recovery position** (on his side) to prevent choking on vomit [S6].
3.  **Monitor:** Keep an eye on him until he fully recovers or medical help arrives if advised by a professional.

**Warning Signs:** Seek immediate professional medical help if he experiences any of the following:
*   Returns to unresponsiveness.
*   Breathing becomes irregular, stops, or turns into gasps [S2].
*   Severe chest pain, confusion, or slurred speech.
*   Any signs of shock (pale, cold, clammy skin) [S6].

*Note: This information is for general guidance and does not replace professional medical advice.*

sources.text:
**Adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally:**

1. Call for help and an AED (defibrillator) if one exists.
2. Hands stacked on the **center of the chest** (lower half of the breastbone), arms straight.
3. Compress **5 to 6 cm** deep, **100 to 120 times per minute** (the rhythm of the song "Stayin' Alive"), letting the chest come back up fully between compressions.
4. If trained: 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths. If not: **continuous compressions only**.
5. Don't stop until the person starts breathing again, help arrives or you are exhausted. Take turns every 2 minutes if there are more people.

**Child (1 year to puberty):** one or two hands, depth of about 1/3 of the chest (~5 cm). **Infant (<1 year):** two fingers, about 4 cm. In children and drowning victims, rescue breaths are especially important.

> Source: American Heart Association — *2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care* (and updates). https://cpr.heart.org

sources.section: Order of CPR in a first aid sequence
heading_path: Order of CPR in a first aid sequence
sources.text:
The best position for CPR maneuvers in the sequence of first aid reactions to a cardiac arrest is a question that has been long studied.[17][18]

As a general reference, the recommended order (according to the guidelines of many related associations such as AHA and Red Cross) is:

1. Asking for help from bystanders in case any of them have received first aid training or can perform additional tasks.
   - Variation: when the rescuer is alone and no phone is nearby, the rescuer would go first for a phone to call for emergency medical services[17] (only if the rescuer can return in very few minutes to apply CPR maneuvers to the patient, or emergency medical services will be with the patient in a few minutes).
2. Calling by phone for emergency medical services. Also, go for an automated defibrillator (AED), but only if the AED is available within a few minutes.
3. Attempting defibrillation with the automated external defibrillator (AED), because it is easy to use if it has been found. If not, or until it has arrived, attempting CPR maneuvers as the latest step of those possible ones.

If there are multiple rescuers, these tasks can be distributed and performed simultaneously to save time.

sources.text:
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation
CPR being performed on a medical-training mannequin
Specialty | Cardiology, emergency medicine, critical care medicine
ICD-9 | 99.60
MeSH | D016887
OPS-301 code | 8-771
MedlinePlus | 000010

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is an emergency procedure used during cardiac or respiratory arrest that involves chest compressions, often combined with artificial ventilation, to preserve brain function and maintain circulation until spontaneous breathing and heartbeat can be restored. It is recommended for those who are unresponsive with no breathing or abnormal breathing, for example, agonal respirations.[1]

CPR involves chest compressions for adults between 5 cm (2.0 in) and 6 cm (2.4 in) deep and at a rate of at least 100 to 120 per minute.[2] The rescuer may also provide artificial ventilation by either exhaling air into the subject's mouth or nose (mouth-to-mouth resuscitation) or using a device that pushes air into the subject's lungs (mechanical ventilation). Current recommendations emphasize early and high-quality chest compressions over artificial ventilation; a simplified CPR method involving only chest compressions is recommended for untrained rescuers.[3] With children, however, 2015 American Heart Association guidelines indicate that doing only compressions may result in worse outcomes, because such problems in children normally arise from respiratory issues rather than from cardiac ones, given their young age.[1] Chest compression to breathing ratios are set at 30 to 2 in adults.

CPR alone is unlikely to restart the heart. Its main purpose is to restore the partial flow of oxygenated blood to the brain and heart. The objective is to delay tissue death and to extend the brief window of opportunity for a successful resuscitation without permanent brain damage. Administration of an electric shock to the subject's heart, termed defibrillation, is usually needed to restore a viable, or "perfusing", heart rhythm. Defibrillation is effective only for certain heart rhythms, namely ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, rather than asystole or pulseless electrical activity, which usually requires the treatment of underlying conditions to restore cardiac function. Early shock, when appropriate, is recommended. CPR may succeed in inducing a heart rhythm that may be shockable. In general, CPR is continued until the person has a return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) or is declared dead.[4]

sources.original_text:
An automated external defibrillator stored in a visible orange mural support

Defibrillation is indicated if a shockable rhythm is present; the two shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. These shockable rhythms have a 25-40% likelihood of survival, compared with a significantly lower rate (less than 5%) in non-shockable rhythms.[96] The non-shockable rhythms include asystole and pulseless electrical activity.

Ventricular fibrillation involves the ventricles of the heart rapidly contracting in an disorganized pattern, and thereby limiting blood flow from the heart. This is due to an uncoordinated electrical activity.[97] The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows irregular QRS complexes at a very high rate (>300 beats per minute).[98] In ventricular tachycardia, the ECG will show a wide complex rhythm at a rate higher than 100 beats per minute.[99] These two rhythm lead to hemodynamic instability and compromise, resulting in poor perfusion to vital organs (including the heart itself).

Demonstration of anterolateral pad placement for defibrillation

A defibrillator — either implanted or external — delivers an electrical current that results in the entire myocardium simultaneously depolarized thereby stopping the arrhythmia.[100] Defibrillators can deliver energy as monophasic or biphasic waveforms, although biphasic defibrillators are now the most common.[101][102] Prior studies suggest that biphasic shock is more likely to produce successful defibrillation after a single shock, however rate of survival is comparable between the methods.[102]

In out-of-hospital arrests (OHCA), the defibrillation is often made by an automated external defibrillator (AED), a portable machine that can be used by any user. The AED provides voice instructions that guide the process, automatically checks the person's condition, and applies the appropriate electric shocks. Some defibrillators even provide feedback on the quality of CPR compressions, encouraging the lay rescuer to press the person's chest hard enough to circulate blood.[103]

There is increasing use of public access to defibrillators. This typically involves placing AEDs in publicly-accessible places and training staff in these areas on how to use them. This allows defibrillation to occur prior to the arrival of emergency services, which has been shown to increase the chances of survival. People who have cardiac arrests in remote locations have worse outcomes.[104]

Defibrillation cannot reverse asystole or pulseless electrical activity, and CPR must be initiated first in these cases. A similar concept, cardioversion, utilizes the same defibrillation machine but is used for other rhythms such as atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia. In these rhythms, the machine is "synchronized" to the QRS complex to avoid shocking on the T wave (and inducing VT or VF). Cardioversion can be done electively for rhythm control, or urgently if the rhythm is unstable.

sources.text:
1. **Is the scene safe?** Don't become a second victim (fire, electricity, traffic, collapse).
2. **Responsive?** Tap the shoulders and call out loudly.
3. **X — eXsanguinating hemorrhage:** severe bleeding? Control it first (see below).
4. **A — airway:** open? Tilt the head and lift the chin (if there is no suspected neck injury).
5. **B — breathing:** look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. No breathing or only "gasps" (gasping) = cardiac arrest → CPR.
6. **C — circulation:** pallor, cold and clammy skin, rapid pulse = shock.
7. **D — level of consciousness (disability).**
8. **E — exposure:** look for other injuries and protect from the cold.

**Recovery position:** an unconscious person who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed on their side so they don't choke on vomit.

> Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) — *International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020*.

Current recommendations emphasize early and high-quality chest compressions over artificial ventilation; a simplified CPR method involving only chest compressions is recommended for untrained rescuers.[3] With children, however, 2015 American Heart Association guidelines indicate that doing only compressions may result in worse outcomes, because such problems in children normally arise from respiratory issues rather than from cardiac ones, given their young age.[1] Chest compression to breathing ratios are set at 30 to 2 in adults.

CPR alone is unlikely to restart the heart. Its main purpose is to restore the partial flow of oxygenated blood to the brain and heart. The objective is to delay tissue death and to extend the brief window of opportunity for a successful resuscitation without permanent brain damage. Administration of an electric shock to the subject's heart, termed defibrillation, is usually needed to restore a viable, or "perfusing", heart rhythm. Defibrillation is effective only for certain heart rhythms, namely ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, rather than asystole or pulseless electrical activity, which usually requires the treatment of underlying conditions to restore cardiac function. Early shock, when appropriate, is recommended. CPR may succeed in inducing a heart rhythm that may be shockable. In general, CPR is continued until the person has a return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) or is declared dead.[4]

sources.title: Cardiac arrest
sources.text: Open the full source below. This section is unavailable or too long to include safely as a complete passage.
sources.original_text:
An automated external defibrillator stored in a visible orange mural support

Defibrillation is indicated if a shockable rhythm is present; the two shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. These shockable rhythms have a 25-40% likelihood of survival, compared with a significantly lower rate (less than 5%) in non-shockable rhythms.[96] The non-shockable rhythms include asystole and pulseless electrical activity.

Ventricular fibrillation involves the ventricles of the heart rapidly contracting in an disorganized pattern, and thereby limiting blood flow from the heart. This is due to an uncoordinated electrical activity.[97] The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows irregular QRS complexes at a very high rate (>300 beats per minute).[98] In ventricular tachycardia, the ECG will show a wide complex rhythm at a rate higher than 100 beats per minute.[99] These two rhythm lead to hemodynamic instability and compromise, resulting in poor perfusion to vital organs (including the heart itself).

Demonstration of anterolateral pad placement for defibrillation

A defibrillator — either implanted or external — delivers an electrical current that results in the entire myocardium simultaneously depolarized thereby stopping the arrhythmia.[100] Defibrillators can deliver energy as monophasic or biphasic waveforms, although biphasic defibrillators are now the most common.[101][102] Prior studies suggest that biphasic shock is more likely to produce successful defibrillation after a single shock, however rate of survival is comparable between the methods.[102]

In out-of-hospital arrests (OHCA), the defibrillation is often made by an automated external defibrillator (AED), a portable machine that can be used by any user. The AED provides voice instructions that guide the process, automatically checks the person's condition, and applies the appropriate electric shocks. Some defibrillators even provide feedback on the quality of CPR compressions, encouraging the lay rescuer to press the person's chest hard enough to circulate blood.[103]

There is increasing use of public access to defibrillators. This typically involves placing AEDs in publicly-accessible places and training staff in these areas on how to use them. This allows defibrillation to occur prior to the arrival of emergency services, which has been shown to increase the chances of survival. People who have cardiac arrests in remote locations have worse outcomes.[104]

Defibrillation cannot reverse asystole or pulseless electrical activity, and CPR must be initiated first in these cases. A similar concept, cardioversion, utilizes the same defibrillation machine but is used for other rhythms such as atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia. In these rhythms, the machine is "synchronized" to the QRS complex to avoid shocking on the T wave (and inducing VT or VF). Cardioversion can be done electively for rhythm control, or urgently if the rhythm is unstable.

1. **Is the scene safe?** Don't become a second victim (fire, electricity, traffic, collapse).
2. **Responsive?** Tap the shoulders and call out loudly.
3. **X — eXsanguinating hemorrhage:** severe bleeding? Control it first (see below).
4. **A — airway:** open? Tilt the head and lift the chin (if there is no suspected neck injury).
5. **B — breathing:** look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. No breathing or only "gasps" (gasping) = cardiac arrest → CPR.
6. **C — circulation:** pallor, cold and clammy skin, rapid pulse = shock.
7. **D — level of consciousness (disability).**
8. **E — exposure:** look for other injuries and protect from the cold.

**Recovery position:** an unconscious person who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed on their side so they don't choke on vomit.

> Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) — *International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020*.

### Boiling (most reliable method)

- Bring the water to a **rolling boil (bubbling) for 1 minute**.
- Above 2,000 m altitude, boil for **3 minutes**.
- Let it cool covered. To improve the taste, pour it back and forth between containers a few times (adds oxygen).

> Source: CDC — Making Water Safe in an Emergency. https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html

### Household bleach / hypochlorite (chlorine)

Use only bleach that is **unscented, without color-safe bleach and without additives**, within its expiry date (chlorine loses strength with time and heat).

| Product | Dose per liter of clear water | Waiting time |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium hypochlorite 2.5% (bottle distributed free by Brazil's public health system, SUS) | 2 drops | 30 minutes |
| Common household bleach 2.0–2.5% ("água sanitária" in Brazil) | 2 drops | 30 minutes |
| Bleach 6% (US standard) | 2 drops (8 drops per gallon) | 30 minutes |
| Bleach 8.25% | 1–2 drops (6 drops per gallon) | 30 minutes |

- Cloudy or very cold water: **double the dose** and wait longer.
- After 30 minutes there should be a **slight smell of chlorine**. If there isn't, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.

> Sources: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — guidance on using 2.5% sodium hypochlorite in water for human consumption; CDC — Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water. https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water

### SODIS — solar disinfection

1. Use **clear PET bottles, label removed, up to 2 liters**, without heavy scratches.
2. The water must be clear (you can read large letters through the full bottle).
3. Lay the bottles down in full sun, preferably on a roof tile or metal sheet.
4. **6 hours** of strong sun; **2 consecutive days** if the sky is more than half cloudy.
5. Does not work well in continuous rain.

> Source: Eawag/SANDEC — SODIS Manual. https://www.sodis.ch

### Commercial filters and tablets

- Ceramic or membrane filters (0.1–0.2 micron) remove bacteria and protozoa; most **do not remove viruses**. Combine with chlorine when the water comes from areas with sewage.
- Sodium dichloroisocyanurate (NaDCC) or chlorine dioxide tablets: follow the package instructions.
- Household clay (candle) filters improve water but do not replace boiling/chlorine for high-risk water.
